scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The `adaptyv` skill is a documentation-only reference for the Adaptyv Bio Foundry REST API and Python SDK. It contains no script files, no obfuscated content, no eval/exec or shell-injection patterns, and no exfiltration of local data: all network endpoints referenced belong to the vendor's own documented API domains (docs.adaptyvbio.com, foundry-api-public.adaptyvbio.com). Credential guidance is sound (environment variables, no hardcoding, no committing tokens) and no secrets are embedded. The activation description is keyword-rich but accurately scoped to the vendor's product, so it does not constitute capability inflation. Residual issues are minor hygiene concerns: an unpinned git-based dependency install, a documented auto-accept-quote automation pattern that could incur real costs without user confirmation, guidance to load .env files, and several dangling file references. Overall the skill appears benign.
llm_primary_threats: Autonomous financial commitment via auto-accept-quote pattern

findings.title: Instruction to locate and load .env secrets files
findings.description: The skill directs the agent to look for a `.env` file in the project root and load it to obtain the API token. While this is a common and legitimate credential-handling pattern (and the skill correctly warns against hardcoding or committing tokens), it does broaden the agent's interaction with secret-bearing files, which could surface unrelated secrets from that file into the agent context.
findings.snippet: Check for a `.env` file in the project root first; if one exists, use a library like `python-dotenv` to load it.
findings.remediation: Instruct the agent to read only the specific `ADAPTYV_API_KEY` variable, avoid echoing the value or other .env contents, and prefer environment variables over parsing secret files.

findings.title: Documented automation pattern bypasses human review of financial commitment
findings.description: The skill documents an 'Automated Pipeline' pattern that sets `skip_draft: true` and `auto_accept_quote: true`, which bypasses the Draft review stage and automatically accepts a paid quote and creates a Stripe invoice. If an agent follows this example without explicit user confirmation, it can commit the user to real laboratory costs autonomously. The skill does not include a caution to obtain user confirmation before enabling auto-accept.
findings.snippet:
exp = client.experiments.create({
    "name": "Auto pipeline run",
    "experiment_spec": {...},
    "skip_draft": True,
    "auto_accept_quote": True,
    "webhook_url": "https://my-server.com/webhook"
})
findings.remediation: Add an explicit instruction that the agent must obtain user confirmation (and show the cost estimate) before using `skip_draft` or `auto_accept_quote`, and default examples to Draft-first workflows.

findings.title: Unpinned dependency installed directly from GitHub
findings.description: The skill instructs the agent to install the `adaptyv-sdk` package directly from a GitHub repository with no version, tag, or commit pin (`git+https://github.com/adaptyvbio/adaptyv-sdk.git`). Any future compromise of, or force-push to, the default branch of that repository would result in arbitrary code being installed and executed in the user's environment. The repository appears to be the vendor's official org, which lowers risk, but the lack of provenance pinning is a supply-chain weakness.
findings.snippet:
uv pip install "git+https://github.com/adaptyvbio/adaptyv-sdk.git"
uv add "adaptyv-sdk @ git+https://github.com/adaptyvbio/adaptyv-sdk.git"
findings.remediation: Pin the install to an immutable ref (e.g., `@v0.1.0` tag or a full commit SHA) and prefer a PyPI release with hash verification once available. Note the expected publisher/fingerprint in the skill docs.

findings.title: Missing referenced files and unspecified allowed-tools
findings.description: The skill package references `adaptyv.py`, `templates/api-endpoints.md`, and `assets/api-endpoints.md`, none of which exist in the package (only `references/api-endpoints.md` is present). Broken references can lead the agent to search the filesystem or fabricate content. Additionally, `allowed-tools` is not declared (optional per spec, informational only) for a skill that implies network/HTTP and package-install activity.
findings.snippet: Referenced File: adaptyv.py (not found); templates/api-endpoints.md (not found); assets/api-endpoints.md (not found)
findings.remediation: Remove or fix dangling file references and declare `allowed-tools` explicitly (e.g., Read, Bash/Python) so tool usage matches documented behavior.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The antibody-engineering skill is a self-contained, offline bioinformatics utility and appears benign. All three Python scripts (number_antibody.py, scan_liabilities.py, physchem_profile.py) perform local sequence parsing, regex motif matching, and arithmetic on amino-acid sequences. There are no network calls, no subprocess/os.system/eval/exec usage, no reading of credential paths (~/.aws, ~/.ssh), no environment-variable harvesting, no hardcoded secrets, no base64/hex-obfuscated payloads, and no filesystem traversal beyond user-specified input paths and an explicit --out file. File writes are limited to the user-provided --out argument, consistent with the declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash). The SKILL.md body contains no prompt-injection, role-redefinition, concealment, or safety-bypass language; it is technical documentation that in fact encourages conservative reporting ('say no sequence liabilities detected, structure-based properties not assessed'). Bundled reference markdown files are internal to the package and contain only domain guidance. Dependencies (anarci, HMMER) are named legitimate bioinformatics packages installed by the user, not auto-installed by the scripts; they are unpinned, which is a minor supply-chain hygiene note rather than an active threat. Only two low-severity, informational observations were identified.

findings.title: Trigger keyword list in description broadens activation surface
findings.description: The YAML description ends with an explicit activation directive listing many trigger terms ('Also trigger on antibody, nanobody, VHH, scFv, Fab, CDR, framework, ANARCI, abnumber, IgBLAST, OAS, SAbDab, humanization, Vernier residues, or developability'). All listed keywords are genuinely within the skill's stated antibody-engineering domain, so this is not deceptive capability inflation, but the pattern does deliberately maximise discovery/activation and could cause the skill to load in loosely related conversations. Informational only.
findings.snippet: Also trigger on antibody, nanobody, VHH, scFv, Fab, CDR, framework, ANARCI, abnumber, IgBLAST, OAS, SAbDab, humanization, Vernier residues, or developability.
findings.remediation: Keep the description scoped to the actual capabilities and avoid explicit 'trigger on <keyword list>' directives; rely on natural description matching.

findings.title: Some referenced documentation paths do not exist in the package
findings.description: The instruction body references four reference documents; three of the four (references/numbering-schemes.md, references/developability.md, references/humanization-and-design.md, references/tools.md) are present. The scanner additionally probed templates/ and assets/ variants that are absent. No missing file is actually required by the instructions, and no external URLs or user-supplied files are fetched or executed, so the risk is documentation-completeness only, not indirect prompt injection.
findings.snippet: Read [references/numbering-schemes.md](references/numbering-schemes.md) ... [references/tools.md](references/tools.md)
findings.remediation: Ensure all referenced paths resolve within the package; remove or correct any stale links.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The autodock-vina skill is a legitimate computational-chemistry helper for AutoDock Vina / Meeko workflows. All three bundled Python scripts (make_box.py, dock_batch.py, parse_vina_output.py) use only the standard library, parse structure/output files locally, and invoke external docking binaries via subprocess with argument lists (no shell=True, no eval/exec, no string interpolation into a shell). There are no network calls, no credential or environment-variable access, no hardcoded secrets, no obfuscated or encoded payloads, and no file access outside user-supplied paths and the declared output directory. Subprocess calls include explicit timeouts, a --dry-run mode, and a `check` subcommand, and worker parallelism is bounded by an explicit --workers flag, so no resource-exhaustion pattern is evident. The SKILL.md body and the bundled reference documents (receptor-preparation.md, ligand-preparation.md, scoring-and-interpretation.md, troubleshooting.md) contain only domain guidance; there are no instruction-override, concealment, safety-bypass, or role-redefinition directives, and no directive to fetch or execute content from external URLs (the only URLs are documentation links). Declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash) are consistent with the actual behavior: reading structure files, writing config/PDB/TSV outputs, and running the vina/Meeko CLIs. The description's list of trigger terms (vina, smina, gnina, PDBQT, etc.) is narrowly scoped to the skill's actual domain and does not constitute capability inflation. Referenced files under assets/ and templates/ resolve to the same names under references/, which exist; the missing duplicates are a path-resolution artifact rather than a security issue. No security findings warranting remediation were identified.

The skill is a legitimate, well-documented bioinformatics helper for the open-source Boltz-2 cofolding model, and its behaviour matches its manifest. All three bundled Python scripts use only the standard library: make_boltz_yaml.py emits a YAML document from argparse-validated flags, screen_library.py fans a SMILES file out into per-ligand YAMLs plus a manifest, and collect_results.py walks a prediction directory and joins JSON confidence/affinity files into a table. There are no network calls, no subprocess/os.system/eval/exec, no shell string interpolation, no hardcoded secrets, no reads of ~/.aws, ~/.ssh, or environment credentials, and no obfuscated or encoded payloads. File writes are confined to user-specified --out/--out-dir paths, and library names are sanitised with a strict allowlist regex before being used as filenames, which mitigates path traversal. The SKILL.md body and both reference files contain no prompt-injection, role-redefinition, concealment, or safety-bypass language; the guidance is unusually conservative (warns about misreading the affinity sign, about low-ipTM poses, about the 128-atom affinity limit, and about sending sequences to a public server). File writes and Bash usage are consistent with the declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash). Only minor, informational issues were found: an activation-keyword list in the description, unpinned/VCS pip install guidance for the upstream package, and the inherent third-party data flow of the optional ColabFold MSA server, which the skill itself discloses. Recommended verdict: safe to use.

findings.title: Trigger-keyword list appended to skill description
findings.description: The YAML description ends with an explicit activation-keyword list ("Also trigger on Boltz, Boltz-1, Boltz-2, cofolding, boltz predict, affinity_pred_value, affinity_probability_binary, ipTM, or open-weights AlphaFold3 alternatives"). This is a discovery-optimisation pattern. In this case all keywords are tightly scoped to the skill's genuine domain (Boltz cofolding/affinity prediction) and there is no brand impersonation or over-broad claim such as "general assistant", so the risk is informational only.
findings.snippet: Also trigger on Boltz, Boltz-1, Boltz-2, cofolding, boltz predict, affinity_pred_value, affinity_probability_binary, ipTM, or open-weights AlphaFold3 alternatives.
findings.remediation: Keep the description to a functional summary; rely on semantic matching rather than an explicit trigger-word list to avoid unnecessary activation.

findings.title: Unpinned dependency install, including direct install from a Git repository
findings.description: references/running.md instructs the user to run `pip install boltz` without a version pin and offers `pip install git+https://github.com/jwohlwend/boltz.git` to obtain the development branch. Unpinned and VCS-HEAD installs mean the executed code is whatever the upstream repository currently contains, so a future upstream compromise would flow directly onto the user's machine. The repository referenced is the genuine upstream project for Boltz and the skill's own bundled scripts have no third-party dependencies, so impact is limited.
findings.snippet:
pip install boltz            # 2.2.1; requires Python >=3.10,<3.13
# or, for the development version
pip install git+https://github.com/jwohlwend/boltz.git
findings.remediation: Pin the tested release (e.g. `pip install boltz==2.2.1`) and, if a development install is offered, pin it to a specific commit hash. Recommend installing into an isolated virtual environment.

findings.title: Documented workflow transmits input sequences to a third-party public server
findings.description: The recommended `boltz predict ... --use_msa_server` workflow sends the user's protein sequence to the public ColabFold MSA server, i.e. local input data crosses a network boundary to a third party. This is inherent to the upstream tool rather than hidden behaviour: the skill's compatibility field, references/yaml-schema.md, references/running.md, and a runtime warning printed by make_boltz_yaml.py all state this explicitly and advise against use with confidential or unpublished sequences. The bundled scripts themselves make no network calls. Noted for awareness of the data-flow only.
findings.snippet: # reminder: no MSA path given, so `boltz predict` must be run with --use_msa_server (which sends your sequence to the public ColabFold server -- do not use it for confidential sequences).
findings.remediation: No change required; the existing warnings are appropriate. Optionally default screening guidance to precomputed MSAs (`--msa-path`) or a self-hosted `--msa_server_url` so that no sequence leaves the environment by default.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The `chembl` skill is a well-documented, benign research utility for querying the public ChEMBL REST API at www.ebi.ac.uk. The three Python scripts (`compound_lookup.py`, `target_activities.py`, `chembl_query.py`) and the shared `_common.py` helper use only the Python standard library, perform read-only HTTP GET requests to the documented ChEMBL endpoints, and write results to user-specified output files. No prompt-injection, role-redefinition, concealment, or safety-bypass language appears in SKILL.md or the two bundled reference files, which contain only domain-specific cheminformatics guidance. There is no use of eval/exec/os.system/subprocess, no shell invocation, no credential or environment-variable access, no reading of ~/.ssh, ~/.aws or other sensitive paths, no hardcoded secrets, no base64/hex obfuscation, no package installation, and no network destinations other than the EBI API root. File writes are limited to explicit `--out` paths, and paging is bounded by `--max-rows` (default 20000) and `MAX_LIMIT`, with retries capped at 4 attempts and a 30s backoff ceiling, so no resource-exhaustion pattern is present. Declared `allowed-tools` (Read, Write, Edit, Bash) are consistent with observed behaviour, and the description/keyword list, while long, accurately reflects the skill's genuine ChEMBL scope rather than inflating capabilities. Referenced files that were not found (templates/*, assets/*) appear to be scanner path-permutation artifacts of the two real `references/*.md` files, which are bundled internally and safe. The only noted item is the informational, documented `--base-url` override.

findings.title: Configurable API base URL could redirect queries (and query content) to an arbitrary host
findings.description: All bundled scripts expose a `--base-url` flag that defaults to the public EBI endpoint but accepts any URL. `_common._build_url` will pass through any absolute http(s) path unmodified. If an agent is instructed (e.g., by untrusted user text or by a poisoned reference file) to pass a different base URL, the queries — including user-supplied SMILES, target ids, and other search terms — would be sent to a third-party host, and the returned JSON would be written into local TSV/CSV/JSON files. This is a normal, documented convenience feature for mirrors and is not malicious, but it is an unauthenticated outbound-request surface controlled by a plain string argument with no host allow-list.
findings.snippet:
parser.add_argument("--base-url", default=BASE_URL, help="override the API root (default: the public EBI endpoint)")
...
if path.startswith("http://") or path.startswith("https://"):
    return path
findings.remediation: Optionally validate that `--base-url` resolves to an expected host (e.g., restrict to www.ebi.ac.uk or require explicit user confirmation for other hosts), and reject plain http:// schemes.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The datamol skill is a documentation-only cheminformatics wrapper guide. It contains no executable scripts (no .py or .sh files bundled), and all four resolvable reference files (core_api.md, core_workflows.md, io_module.md, conformers_module.md, descriptors_viz.md, fragments_scaffolds.md, reactions_data.md, workflow_patterns.md) contain only legitimate RDKit/datamol API documentation and example code. No prompt injection, instruction override, concealment directives, role redefinition, or system-prompt extraction attempts were found in any language. No hardcoded secrets, no eval/exec/os.system patterns, no reverse shells, no obfuscation or encoded payloads, no external URL fetching of instructions (only documentation links to docs.datamol.io, rdkit.org, and the official GitHub repo). The description accurately matches the content, and declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash) are consistent with the stated need to install packages and read/write molecular files. Only minor, low-severity hygiene issues were identified: unpinned pip installs, documentation of cloud credential env vars with remote-write examples (accompanied by explicit user-confirmation guardrails), and several referenced file paths that do not exist in the package. Overall risk: LOW; the skill appears benign.

findings.title: Documentation of cloud credential environment variables and remote write paths
findings.description: Reference documentation describes cloud storage I/O via fsspec, naming credential environment variables (AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS) and showing writes to remote S3/GCS destinations. This is legitimate library documentation for datamol and includes explicit mitigations ("Only use cloud paths when the user explicitly requests them", "Confirm the destination before writing", "does not collect or transmit environment variables to third-party endpoints", "Scope credential access to the named provider variables only"). No code reads or transmits these credentials. Flagged informationally only: any remote-write pattern is a potential data egress channel if the agent is later given an attacker-controlled destination.
findings.snippet:
dm.save_df(df, "s3://bucket/output.parquet")  # confirm destination first
Cloud backends read credentials from the standard provider environment (for example `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` ...)
findings.remediation: Keep the existing user-confirmation requirement for any remote read/write; avoid enumerating credential variable names in guidance and never allow destination URLs sourced from untrusted files or model-generated content without explicit user approval.

findings.title: Unpinned dependency installation instructions
findings.description: The skill instructs the agent to install packages via `uv pip install datamol`, `s3fs`, and `gcsfs` without version pinning or hash verification. While these are legitimate, well-known PyPI packages (datamol-io project), unpinned installs create a minor supply-chain exposure if a registry or package is compromised. No GitHub/unknown-repo installs or typosquatted names were detected.
findings.snippet:
uv pip install datamol
uv pip install s3fs   # AWS S3
uv pip install gcsfs  # Google Cloud Storage
findings.remediation: Pin versions explicitly (e.g., `uv pip install datamol==0.12.5`) and prompt the user for confirmation before installing packages into their environment.

findings.title: Missing/unresolved referenced files (broken provenance surface)
findings.description: The extracted reference list includes many paths that do not exist in the package (assets/*.md, templates/*.md, plus 'sklearn.py' and 'datamol.py'). The SKILL.md body explicitly clarifies that scipy/scikit-learn are PyPI packages and not bundled scripts, and the 'sklearn.py'/'datamol.py' entries appear to be artifacts of import-statement parsing rather than real files. No malicious content is present, but unresolved reference paths could allow a later-added file at those paths to be loaded implicitly (indirect instruction surface).
findings.snippet:
Referenced File: assets/core_api.md (not found)
Referenced File: sklearn.py (not found)
Referenced File: datamol.py (not found)
findings.remediation: Ensure the reference list matches only files actually bundled under references/, and remove/ignore ambiguous names that collide with third-party module names to avoid accidental local file shadowing.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The deepchem skill appears benign and consistent with its stated purpose. SKILL.md contains only legitimate technical documentation for molecular machine learning — there are no prompt-injection attempts, instruction overrides, concealment directives, or role redefinitions in any language. The three bundled Python scripts (predict_solubility.py, graph_neural_network.py, transfer_learning.py) use only argparse plus the deepchem API: no eval/exec, no subprocess/os.system, no filesystem traversal, no reading of credential paths (~/.aws, ~/.ssh), no environment-variable harvesting, no hardcoded secrets, no outbound POST/exfiltration endpoints, and no obfuscated or encoded payloads. File access is limited to user-specified CSV paths passed as explicit CLI arguments, and all referenced documentation files are internal to the skill package (several referenced paths under assets/ and templates/ simply do not exist, which is a harmless documentation artifact). Declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash) are consistent with training scripts that write model directories such as ./grover_pretrained. Remaining findings are low-severity hygiene issues: unpinned/nightly dependency installation guidance, automatic download of third-party pretrained checkpoints, undisclosed network egress in the compatibility metadata, and unbounded default training compute.

findings.title: Undeclared network access despite compatibility metadata omitting it
findings.description: The skill's scripts perform network operations (MoleculeNet dataset downloads via dc.molnet.load_* and Hugging Face model downloads) and the instructions include pip/conda installation commands, but the `compatibility` field only mentions Python/backend requirements and does not disclose outbound network usage. This is a minor manifest/behavior transparency gap rather than deceptive capability inflation; the description accurately reflects the skill's molecular-ML purpose.
findings.snippet:
compatibility: Requires Python 3.7–3.11 ... RDKit is a core dependency.
(scripts call dc.molnet.load_tox21(...) and dc.models.HuggingFaceModel(model='seyonec/...'), which download remote data/weights)
findings.remediation: Explicitly state in the manifest/compatibility notes that the skill requires outbound network access to download benchmark datasets and pretrained model weights.

findings.title: Unpinned dependency installation instructions including nightly pre-release builds
findings.description: SKILL.md instructs the agent to install packages via `uv pip install deepchem`, `uv pip install 'deepchem[torch]'`, `conda install "mkl<2025"`, and even nightly pre-release builds via `uv pip install --pre deepchem` without any version pinning. Unpinned/pre-release installs expose the environment to supply-chain risk (malicious or broken package versions) and non-reproducible builds. This is standard documentation practice for ML libraries, so risk is low, but the `--pre` nightly recommendation is notable.
findings.snippet:
uv pip install deepchem
uv pip install 'deepchem[torch]'
Nightly builds: `uv pip install --pre deepchem`
findings.remediation: Pin explicit versions (e.g. `deepchem==2.8.0`) consistent with the stated version note, and avoid recommending nightly `--pre` builds by default. Require explicit user confirmation before any package installation.

findings.title: Long-running compute-intensive training defaults without resource guardrails
findings.description: Scripts default to 50 epochs of GNN/regressor training (and 10-20 epochs of transformer fine-tuning) on datasets such as Tox21/HIV, which can consume substantial CPU/GPU time and memory when invoked by an agent. There is no timeout, sample cap, or user confirmation prompt. This is expected behavior for an ML training skill and is user-parameterized (--epochs), so severity is low.
findings.snippet:
parser.add_argument('--epochs', type=int, default=50, help='Number of training epochs')
model.fit(train, nb_epoch=50)
findings.remediation: Lower default epoch counts for agent-driven runs, add optional max-runtime/max-sample limits, and note expected resource cost in the skill instructions so the agent can confirm with the user before long jobs.

findings.title: Automatic download and execution of remote pretrained model weights
findings.description: scripts/transfer_learning.py loads third-party pretrained checkpoints from Hugging Face Hub identifiers ('seyonec/ChemBERTa-zinc-base-v1', 'ibm/MoLFormer-XL-both-10pct') and GROVER weights, which triggers network downloads of remote model artifacts on first run. Remote model artifacts (especially pickle-based checkpoints) are a recognized supply-chain vector. The identifiers are well-known public models and are hardcoded (not user-controlled), so the risk is limited.
findings.snippet:
'model_id': 'seyonec/ChemBERTa-zinc-base-v1'
'model_id': 'ibm/MoLFormer-XL-both-10pct'
print("(This may take a while on the first run as the model is downloaded)")
findings.remediation: Document the network egress requirement, pin model revisions/commit hashes, and prefer safetensors-format weights to avoid arbitrary code execution during checkpoint deserialization.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The depmap skill is a documentation-oriented bioinformatics reference for querying the Broad Institute's Cancer Dependency Map. It contains no script files, no prompt-injection or instruction-override language, no concealment directives, no credential or environment-variable access, no eval/exec/os.system usage, no obfuscation or encoded payloads, and no hardcoded secrets. All network endpoints referenced (depmap.org, figshare.com, github.com/broadinstitute) are legitimate and consistent with the stated purpose, and the data flow is strictly inbound (download public datasets, analyze locally) with no outbound transmission of user data. The name and description accurately match the documented behavior; there is no capability inflation or keyword baiting beyond legitimate domain terminology. Only minor hygiene issues were identified: a generic URL-to-disk download helper without domain/path validation, missing optional allowed-tools/compatibility metadata despite network and file-write behavior, and an unbounded O(n) correlation loop. The single 'referenced file' flagged (scipy.py) is a false positive from an import statement, not an actual bundled file. Overall risk: LOW.

findings.title: Downloading and writing remote data files to local disk without validation
findings.description: The skill includes example code that downloads arbitrary URLs via requests and streams the content directly to a local file path (download_depmap_data). While the intended sources are legitimate (depmap.org, figshare.com), the helper accepts any URL and output path, and the FILES dict contains a placeholder URL. findings.title: Memory/CPU intensive full-graph load and O(n^2) two-hop path expansion
findings.description: `_load_kg()` reads a ~4 million-row CSV fully into memory (hundreds of MB) and caches it. `find_paths` with max_depth=2 performs nested iterrows over all first- and second-hop edges for each shared intermediate; for hub nodes (e.g., highly connected proteins) this can produce a combinatorial explosion of paths and consume large CPU/memory. This appears to be a performance characteristic rather than intentional abuse — the author bounds depth to 1 or 2 and clears the cache to avoid holding multiple frames — but there is no cap on the number of returned paths.

scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The pytdc skill is a well-constructed, defensively engineered wrapper around the official Therapeutics Data Commons Python package. scan_metadata.llm_overall_assessment: The 'torchdrug' skill is a documentation/reference package that provides guidance for building TorchDrug 0.2.1 machine learning workflows. It contains no executable script files; all content consists of SKILL.md instructions and reference markdown files with illustrative Python/Bash code snippets. No prompt injection, instruction override, concealment directives, or role redefinition attempts were detected in any human language. Installation commands use pinned versions (torch==2.0.0, torch-scatter==2.1.1, torch-cluster==1.6.1, torchdrug==0.2.1) sourced from official PyG/PyPI indexes, which is good supply-chain hygiene. Network references point only to legitimate upstream documentation (torchdrug.ai, github.com/DeepGraphLearning) and are cited as reading material, not as instructions to fetch and execute remote content. No credential access, environment variable harvesting, data exfiltration, eval/exec, obfuscation, or over-collection patterns are present. Declared allowed-tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash) are consistent with the skill's purpose of generating/debugging code and running version checks, and the description accurately matches the observed content. Several referenced files (assets/*, templates/*, torch.py, torchdrug.py) were not found, but these appear to be false-positive extractions from code snippets and generic path patterns rather than missing malicious payloads; the actual references/*.md files referenced in the reference index are present and benign. The reference material additionally includes responsible-use guidance for generated chemistry and biomedical predictions, which is a positive safety signal.

This is a legitimate, well-engineered bioinformatics retrieval skill. All network endpoints are hardcoded module-level constants pointing exclusively to the public, unauthenticated services declared in the manifest (rest.uniprot.org, search.rcsb.org, data.rcsb.org, files.rcsb.org, alphafold.ebi.ac.uk) — there is no attacker-controlled or dynamically constructed host, and no outbound transmission of local data (only accessions, queries, and user-supplied sequences are sent). The scripts use only the Python standard library, with no dependency installation, no pip/npm/GitHub installs, and no supply-chain surface. There is no eval/exec/os.system/subprocess, no shell invocation, no os.walk of home directories, no reading of ~/.aws, ~/.ssh, environment variables, or credential files, and no hardcoded secrets. No obfuscation, base64 blobs, or hidden stagers are present. The SKILL.md body and both bundled reference files contain only domain-appropriate technical guidance: no instruction overrides, no jailbreak or role-redefinition language, no concealment directives, and no instructions to fetch and execute external content. The referenced files that resolve (references/uniprot-api.md, references/rcsb-search.md, references/choosing-a-structure.md) are internal to the package and benign; the additional 'not found' paths under templates/ and assets/ appear to be scanner-generated path guesses rather than genuine broken references. findings.title: Unbounded pagination and download size with no byte cap
findings.description: `uniprot_pages` follows `Link: rel="next"` headers in an unbounded `while url:` loop, and `download()` reads the full HTTP body into memory before writing to disk. A very large query result or an unexpectedly large structure file could consume substantial memory, bandwidth, or time. Mitigations are present (per-request 90s timeout, max 4 attempts with capped 30s backoff, a bounded 3-round gzip decompression loop, and `--limit` defaults of 25-100 rows), so practical DoS risk is low, and there is no infinite retry or spin.
findings.remediation: Add a maximum page count to `uniprot_pages` and stream downloads in chunks with a configurable maximum byte size.

findings.title: Unvalidated user-supplied path in file write/append destinations
findings.description: Several commands write to caller-supplied paths without normalization or containment checks: `uniprot_fetch.py fasta --out` opens the path in append mode, and `fetch_structure.py` creates arbitrary directories via `Path(args.out_dir).mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)` and writes downloaded bytes there. A path such as `--out ~/.ssh/authorized_keys` or `--out-dir ../../` would append/overwrite outside the working directory. This is a normal CLI convention rather than malicious behavior, and the written content is remote biological data, but the agent should not pass unvalidated paths. Note the manifest declares `Write` and `Edit`, so file creation itself is within the declared tool scope.

with open(args.out, "a", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
    handle.write(text)
...
out_dir = Path(args.out_dir)
out_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
findings.remediation: Resolve and validate output paths against an allowed base directory, reject `..` traversal, and prefer non-append/exclusive writes or explicit overwrite confirmation.
